summary: Ireland is not in the Schengen Area and runs its own visa policy: EU/EEA and Swiss citizens have freedom of movement, British citizens enjoy the Common Travel Area, visitors from the US, Canada, Australia, Japan and many other countries get up to 90 days visa-free with no ETA or pre-registration, and visa nationals apply for a short stay 'C' visa (€60 single entry).

US.notes: Visa-free for up to 90 days — no visa, no ETA, no pre-registration. The immigration officer at the border decides the exact permission granted; be ready to explain your plans and show onward travel.

GB.notes: Common Travel Area: British citizens can live, work and travel in Ireland without any visa or permission, and are not subject to routine passport control arriving from the UK — but airlines still require photo ID, and a passport is the safest document to carry.

fee.notes: €60 for single entry, €100 for multiple entry; some nationalities and categories are fee-exempt. Apply online via the AVATS system, then submit your passport and documents as instructed.

source.name: Irish Immigration Service — Coming to visit Ireland

passportValidity.text: Ireland has no 6-month passport rule — your passport (or, for EU/EEA/Swiss citizens, national ID card) simply needs to be valid for the whole of your stay.

source.name: Citizens Information — Visa requirements for entering Ireland

travelInsurance.text: Travel insurance is not an entry requirement, though visa applicants are advised to hold medical cover. EU citizens can use the EHIC card for necessary public healthcare; everyone else should carry private medical cover.

source.name: Irish Immigration Service — Coming to visit Ireland

onwardTicket.text: Not a formal requirement, but immigration officers at the border may ask non-EEA visitors about return or onward travel, accommodation and funds before granting permission to enter.

source.name: Irish Immigration Service — Coming to visit Ireland

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is published, but non-EEA visitors must satisfy the immigration officer that they can support themselves for the visit — bank statements or cash/cards evidence helps if asked.

source.name: Irish Immigration Service — Coming to visit Ireland

currencyLimits.text: Cash of EUR 10,000 or more must be declared when entering or leaving the EU via Ireland; there are no controls on cash carried between Ireland and other EU countries.

source.name: Revenue — Irish Tax and Customs, travelling to Ireland

notes: Arriving from outside the EU: duty-free allowance of 200 cigarettes, 1 litre of spirits (or 4 litres of wine), and other goods up to €430 per adult arriving by air or sea.
Meat, dairy and most animal products may not be brought in from outside the EU; arrivals from within the EU face no routine customs limits for personal use.

payments.text: Contactless cards and phone payments are accepted almost everywhere, including buses (or use a Leap Card in Dublin); cash is rarely needed beyond small rural pubs, markets and tips.

safety.text: Ireland is one of Europe's safest destinations. The main risks are petty — pickpocketing in Dublin's tourist spots and occasional car break-ins at scenic viewpoints; don't leave valuables visible in rental cars.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Ireland Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: May to September brings the mildest weather and up to 17 hours of daylight in midsummer — but pack rain gear whatever the month; Irish weather changes by the hour.

idp.text: Ireland is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1968 Vienna one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognise is the 1949 Geneva version. A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here.

source.name: UN Treaty Collection — Convention on Road Traffic (Geneva, 1949), status of parties
source.instrument: Convention on Road Traffic, Geneva, 19 September 1949 (UNTS vol. 125, p. 3)

driving.text: Ireland is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1968 Vienna one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognise is the 1949 Geneva version. A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national licence, and for how long a foreign licence may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Ireland yet.

source.name: UN Treaty Collection — Convention on Road Traffic (Geneva, 1949), status of parties

tips.text: Ireland is NOT in the Schengen Area — a Schengen visa is not valid for Ireland, and time spent in Ireland doesn't count against your 90/180 Schengen allowance. Visa nationals need a separate Irish visa (or an eligible BIVS-endorsed UK visa).

Arriving from the UK there are usually no routine passport checks (Common Travel Area), but airlines and ferries require photo ID and immigration officers can still carry out checks — non-Irish/non-British citizens should always carry their passport, and visa nationals need an Irish visa even when entering from the UK.

Driving is on the LEFT, most rentals are manual (automatics cost more — book early), and rural roads on routes like the Ring of Kerry or Wild Atlantic Way are narrow with stone walls — take it slow and use pull-in passing spots.
Expect four seasons in one day: pack waterproof layers year-round rather than an umbrella (Atlantic winds destroy them). Summer rarely exceeds 20°C and winter rarely drops far below freezing.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa or ETA for Ireland?
faq.answer: No visa and no ETA. US citizens simply arrive with a passport valid for their stay and can be admitted for up to 90 days. Unlike the UK, Ireland has no electronic travel authorisation — there is nothing to apply for before travel when flying directly to Ireland.

faq.question: Can I visit Ireland with a Schengen visa?
faq.answer: No. Ireland is not in the Schengen Area and runs its own visa system, so a Schengen visa gives no right to enter Ireland. Visa-required nationals need an Irish short stay 'C' visa — though Chinese and Indian citizens with a UK visa endorsed 'BIVS', and some nationalities under Ireland's Short-stay Visa Waiver Programme with a valid UK visa, can visit without a separate Irish visa.

faq.question: Do I need a UK ETA to travel to Ireland?
faq.answer: Not if you fly directly to Ireland — the UK ETA is a British requirement and Ireland has no equivalent. But if your route transits or enters the UK first (including connecting through London), non-visa-national travellers generally need a UK ETA for that leg, so check UK rules for your itinerary.

faq.question: Do South African citizens need a visa for Ireland?
faq.answer: Yes. Ireland reintroduced the visa requirement for South African passport holders in June 2022, so the old visa-free access no longer applies. South Africans must obtain a short stay 'C' visa (€60 single entry) through the AVATS online system before travelling — allow around 8 weeks.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Ireland as a tourist?
faq.answer: Non-EEA visitors are typically admitted for up to 90 days — the immigration officer stamps the exact permission in your passport at entry. EU/EEA, Swiss and British citizens have no time limit under free movement and the Common Travel Area. Short-stay permissions are generally not extendable for tourism.
